name: Residential Capacity at Launch—Pilot Cohort Scale
consequences: Starting with 8 of 12 possible suites preserves financial runway and allows night technicians to develop safe coverage protocols and event-response procedures before managing more simultaneous participants. However, lower simultaneous census delays event yield accumulation and extends the timeline to reach 50–70 enrolled participants, risking momentum loss if publications lag beyond 24 months or external review triggers early-stage scrutiny.
options: Activate all 12 suites by month 6 and hire a fourth rotating technician to maintain safe 4:1 participant-to-technician ratios during night shifts, accepting higher operational complexity and faster capital draw-down to maximize event capture velocity.

Maintain 8 suites through year one with a fixed 3-technician roster, then add 4 suites conditionally in year two only if the pilot demonstrates zero serious incidents, acceptable data quality, and technician burnout rates below regional overnight-care benchmarks.

Operate 6 suites initially with a single dedicated night technician and a sleep-trained nurse on call, trading lower overhead for reduced simultaneous monitoring depth and slower participant throughput, then scale only if external advisory board endorses the staffing model.
review: Smaller launches reduce operational risk and preserve contingency funds, but risk failing the month-18 threshold of 25 enrolled participants if recruitment or event yield underperforms; scaling decisions rest on metrics (incident rates, data quality, burnout) that only become visible after 6–12 months of operation.

name: Recruitment Pipeline and Inclusivity Boundary
consequences: Strict pre-admission screening (specialist interview, bed-partner collateral, prior PSG, exclusion checklist) ensures clean phenotypes free of epilepsy mimics and untreated sleep apnea, supporting rigorous Aim 2 characterization and reducing false positives in event-triage training. Conversely, narrow criteria shrink the candidate pool in a rare-disorder population, requiring intensive outreach through sleep clinics, neurologist networks, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin—a geographically dispersed referral base that may yield fewer local participants and require travel reimbursement increases.
options: Require prior diagnostic polysomnography documenting at least one parasomnia event and formal sleep medicine specialist sign-off for all candidates, ensuring high phenotypic confidence but limiting recruitment to patients already in hospital systems and potentially creating 3–6 month delays for newly referred cases.

Accept structured clinical interview plus bed-partner collateral as sufficient for entry, with screening PSG conducted in the residential unit itself during the first 2 nights, reducing pre-admission barriers but requiring the facility to absorb screening costs and creating data complexity (screening vs. research-grade nights).

Relax the untreated obstructive sleep apnea exclusion to allow participants with mild OSA (AHI 5–15) who are on treatment, widening the phenotypic pool and boosting enrollment while accepting some confounding of arousal patterns; simultaneously establish a formal sub-group analysis protocol.
review: Strict screening guarantees phenotypic purity but may force months-long recruitment timelines in a small population; relaxing criteria accelerates enrollment but introduces sub-phenotypes that complicate event morphology comparisons and risk diluting the primary Aim 2 findings.

name: Event Yield Target and Stay Duration Strategy
consequences: Planning for 70–80% of participants to capture at least one event during a 2–8 week stay assumes parasomnia frequency aligns with self-reported 2+ episodes per month; the protocol allows up to 10 weeks total with a 2-week extension option for zero-event cases. If actual capture rate falls below 50% by month 18, the enrollment target of 50–70 participants yields insufficient adjudicated events for robust Aim 2 phenotyping, triggering external review and possible recruitment-criteria revision.
options: Set a hard ceiling of 8 weeks per participant regardless of event yield to control per-participant costs and encourage faster enrollment turnover; accept a predicted 10–15% unproductive admission rate and plan extended recruitment to compensate, reserving the protocol-review trigger for true failure conditions.

Extend eligible stay duration to 12 weeks for participants with no captured events after week 8, with blinded technician and participant agreement, betting that longer residence improves yield and justifies the extra compensation (€80/night × 4 weeks = €2,240 per extended case); cap extended admissions at 15% of the cohort to contain cost overruns.

Implement mid-stay structured sleep deprivation or late-night caffeine protocols during week 2 for zero-yield participants, based on clinical evidence that sleep restriction can precipitate confusional arousals and sleep terrors in susceptible individuals; accept increased supervision burden and the risk of confounding the "naturalistic" baseline if deprivation-triggered events morphologically differ from spontaneous ones.
review: Longer stays increase event yield but extend per-participant costs and reduce absolute enrollment number for a fixed budget; shorter stays maximize enrollment velocity but risk missing rare-event phenotypes and triggering month-18 review prematurely.

name: Tiered Sensing Deployment and Technician Annotation Load
consequences: The three-tier model (low-burden nightly + enhanced PSG on 3 nights per stay + escalation nights after technician flagging) aims to balance naturalism with clinical-grade capture without overwhelming the night technician with constant full-PSG scoring. However, real-time annotation of low-burden streams (dry-EEG, mattress, camera, microphone) plus event flagging and escalation-night setup creates variable cognitive load; on busy nights with multiple events, technician task-switching between live monitoring and retrospective scoring can degrade both alertness and annotation quality.
options: Require full PSG montage on nights 1, 3, 5, and 7 of each stay in a rotating schedule, sacrificing some naturalism but providing dense baseline and trend data; task the technician with live annotation only of flagged escalation events, reducing cognitive load and enabling cleaner comparison of enhanced vs. escalation-night morphology.

Deploy a second junior technician trained solely in low-burden stream monitoring and time-stamping on high-event-risk nights, freeing the primary technician to focus on escalation PSG setup and real-time scoring; this adds €20K–30K per year in salary but distributes cognitive load and reduces incident risk from fatigue.

Implement near-real-time automated flagging of probable events using a pretrained motion and arousal-pattern classifier on the low-burden streams, triggering technician review and escalation initiation; accept that the early model may have false-positive rates requiring technician judgment, but offload the initial detection burden from human perception.
review: Denser PSG schedules guarantee richer data but increase technician fatigue and reduce naturalism; automated flagging speeds response but risks false escalations that waste resources and confound the event-triage tool training corpus.

name: Inter-Rater Scoring and Dual-Reviewer Protocol
consequences: The plan mandates two independent raters scoring all annotated nights using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reporting, ensuring transparent adjudication of borderline or equivocal events. This rigor is essential for Aim 2 (phenotyping) and Aim 3 (event-triage benchmarking against gold-standard human agreement). However, dual scoring doubles the person-hours required for annotation, estimated at 2–4 hours per night of raw data across all streams; at 180 nights per year (30 participants × 6 nights average), this is 360–720 hours of specialist reviewing annually, requiring either a dedicated second senior rater or outsourcing to external sleep medicine scorers, adding €40K–60K per year in personnel or consulting costs.
options: Hire a second full-time sleep medicine physician or board-certified technologist by year two, allocating her primarily to independent re-scoring and inter-rater reconciliation; accept the added salary and overhead but establish an internal, stable scoring panel that develops consistent calibration over time and can serve future validation studies.

Use a rotating panel of 3–4 external sleep specialists (board-certified physicians or credentialed technologists from other German sleep centers) on a per-night contract basis, paying ~€150–200 per night for blinded, independent scoring; this avoids fixed salary overhead but introduces inter-rater variability across different external reviewers and requires 6–8 weeks to compile final adjudication scores.

Adopt a single primary scorer (the PI or a dedicated technician) for all nights, with a second reviewer scoring a stratified 30% subset (all flagged events plus a random sample of non-events) to estimate inter-rater agreement and calibrate scoring rules; use the subsample agreement statistic to weight the reliability claims, trading full dual coverage for cost savings of ~50% and acknowledging limited generalizability of inter-rater statistics.
review: Dual scoring guarantees transparent adjudication but creates a proportional annotation labor bottleneck that compounds as enrollment grows; single-reviewer with subsample validation reduces costs but weakens claims of rigorous event ascertainment and may underestimate disagreement on morphologically subtle episodes.

name: Pharmaceutical Partnership and Publication Timeline
consequences: The plan notes pharma partnership as "optional upside" with academic team retaining full publication rights and pharma receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window. If a pharma partner joins by month 6, additional funding (~€400K–600K projected) can accelerate equipment purchases, hiring, and participant compensation, de-risking the year-two target of 30–35 enrolled participants. However, partnership brings governance overhead: steering committee meetings, data access protocols, potential IP disputes over event-triage algorithms, and publication pressure to avoid negative results—if efficacy signals for a partner's candidate drug appear marginal, publication delay or selective reporting risk can erode scientific credibility and grant-funding reputation.
options: Pursue a pharma partnership actively within the first 6 months, negotiate a formal collaboration agreement with explicit publication timelines (6-month post-completion moratorium maximum) and algorithm IP clarity, and use the injected capital to front-load hiring and site setup; plan two co-authored methods papers with pharma scientists to strengthen both credibility and partnership ties.

Defer pharma partnership discussions until year two after the pilot has generated preliminary data on event capture rates and phenotypic findings; this preserves academic independence during early operations and allows negotiation from a position of demonstrated feasibility, but forgoes the early capital infusion and risks slower scaling if DFG funding is delayed.

Establish a formal academic licensing agreement where any event-triage algorithm or phenotypic findings are offered to pharma partners on a non-exclusive, time-limited basis (e.g., 12-month exclusive research license, then public release), avoiding full partnership overhead while generating licensing revenue (~€30K–50K per partner) and enabling multiple pharma sponsors without governance conflicts.
review: Pharma capital accelerates growth but introduces publication governance and IP risks that can undermine academic independence and reputation; deferring partnership preserves autonomy but sacrifices early capital and stretches the break-even point for event yield.

name: External Data Sharing and Repository Deposition Strategy
consequences: The plan restricts public data sharing to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements, explicitly excluding bedroom video due to privacy constraints. Depositing physiological data (EEG, movement, arousal metrics) in a recognized repository (e.g., OpenNeuro, PhysioNet) fulfills the success criterion and maximizes scientific impact via secondary research and algorithm validation by external groups. However, without video, external researchers cannot independently verify event morphology or develop video-based detection methods; this limits the research community's ability to benchmark against the ground truth and delays development of scalable screening tools that rely on accessible home video.
options: Deposit all low-burden sensor streams (dry-EEG, mattress, accelerometry, microphone audio anonymized or redacted) and associated AASM-scored event labels in an open repository by month 30; restrict full PSG and any video data to a managed-access archive requiring data use agreements, reserving the raw video for hypothesis-driven collaborations only.

Develop a synthetic video dataset: create frame-by-frame pose and motion annotations from the raw video (limb angles, torso displacement, arousal markers) without showing faces, and deposit the pose-annotation stream alongside sensor data in the open repository; this enables video-based algorithm development without exposing identifiable imagery, but requires annotation labor (~€20K–30K) and may still carry residual privacy risk.

Segment video into 5-second event-focused clips, apply aggressive face de-identification (blurring, pixelation) and audio redaction, and deposit the de-identified clips under a managed-access framework with institutional review for secondary use; this maximizes the research utility of video morphology but requires legal review and risk acceptance that de-identification may not fully eliminate re-identification under adversarial scrutiny.
review: Open deposition of physiological data alone supports reproducible science and Aim 3 benchmarking but limits external development of video-based detection; video deposition dramatically increases algorithmic utility but introduces privacy risk and legal overhead that may exceed the marginal scientific benefit for a single-site cohort.

name: External Advisory Board Authority and Governance Decision Thresholds
consequences: A 3-member external scientific advisory board reviews progress every 6 months with the PI holding operational authority; budget reallocations above €50K require board approval. This structure ensures scientific accountability and prevents mission drift, but monthly board authority and the €50K threshold create slow decision-making on time-sensitive issues (e.g., emergency equipment replacement, rapid technician hiring for unforeseen expansion opportunity). The month-18 external review trigger (enrollment <25, events <40) provides a formal decision point but does not clarify whether the board can recommend mid-course corrections or must recommend termination.
options: Empower the board to approve emergency operational decisions (equipment, staffing, budget reallocation) up to €100K with 72-hour turnaround and quarterly instead of biannual review, streamlining agility while maintaining oversight; establish a written decision-criteria matrix for month-18 review outcomes (e.g., 15–25 enrolled → revise recruitment, <15 → consider closure) to depoliticize the external review process.

Establish a lightweight steering committee of the PI plus one external board member (rotating) that meets monthly for operational decisions up to €75K and flags only strategic questions (e.g., expansion, partnership, major protocol revisions) to the full board quarterly; this distributes governance burden and accelerates turnaround without diluting external oversight.

Create a formal governance escalation pathway: PI authority up to €50K, executive director (e.g., University Hospital Bonn sleep medicine department head) authority up to €150K, and board approval beyond that; this inserts an institutional layer that can absorb operational decisions and reduce board meeting frequency to quarterly, but may introduce bureaucratic delay if institutional processes move slowly.
review: Tighter governance (more frequent board review, lower approval thresholds) slows operational decisions and may stall emergency responses; delegating more authority to the PI accelerates execution but risks unsupervised budget drift or mission scope creep that the board may not detect until month-18 review.

name: Event Capture Window and Inpatient Duration Trade-Off
consequences: Longer inpatient stays (8–10 weeks) maximize the probability of capturing parasomnia events—raising the denominator for Aim 2 characterization—but increase participant burden, dropout risk, and bed occupancy cost per participant, reducing how many admissions can fit within the 3-year budget. Conversely, capping stays at 2–4 weeks reduces operational friction but risks admitting participants who never exhibit an event, inflating the 20% ceiling on unproductive admissions and forcing protocol amendments.
options: Establish a two-tier admission pathway: intensive 2-week baseline stays for all new participants, with automatic 4-week extension offers only to those demonstrating event capture by night 7, ringfencing extension slots to no more than 40% of total admissions to preserve throughput.

Implement a flexible rolling stay protocol where participants self-select durations from 3–10 weeks at recruitment, stratified by pre-admission event-frequency history, and track whether self-selection biases the sample toward patients with either higher event burden or greater illness conviction.

Use the first 3 months as a calibration phase with intentionally extended 8–10 week stays for the pilot cohort alone, measure actual event-capture rates and attrition, then lock a uniform 4–6 week stay for all subsequent participants regardless of observed baseline frequency.
review: Longer stays improve event yield but compound fixed-bed costs; shorter stays accelerate throughput but risk high unproductive admission rates that trigger protocol review mid-program. The three options do not address how to handle participants who request discharge early due to homesickness or family obligations.

name: Night Technician Role Scope and Staffing Model
consequences: Technicians must perform real-time event annotation, participant safety checks, sensor troubleshooting, and emergency response while monitoring 8 simultaneous suites—a cognitively high-demand role that demands sleep medicine background and cannot be easily outsourced or compressed into fewer staff. Expanding technician responsibilities (e.g., scoring, pre-processing) deepens expertise retention but reduces response time; conversely, hiring junior staff to handle only safety/setup and outsourcing annotation post-hoc lowers wages but fragments context and increases later curation overhead.
options: Recruit senior sleep technicians with PSG credentialing and fund two full-time equivalent night staff to share the 8-suite load (one technician per 4 suites with overlap for incident response), accepting the €400K–500K annual personnel premium as non-negotiable for safe operations and annotation quality.

Hire bachelor's-level research technicians trained only in sensor maintenance and participant safety, with all real-time event flagging and post-hoc scoring delegated to a dedicated day-shift technician and the postdoctoral researchers, trading longer post-collection processing time for 30–40% lower night-shift wages.

Implement a hybrid model where one senior sleep technician and two rotating junior staff work shared nights, with the senior technician on-call via mobile alerts for escalation; reserve senior technician for first-stay nights, intensive event periods, and weekly annotation review, reducing full-time headcount but requiring robust escalation protocols.
review: Higher technician seniority ensures event capture fidelity but locks in high fixed wages; junior staff reduce labor cost but create annotation backlog and risk missed events during low-attention windows. None of the options address how technician turnover—particularly mid-research-year departure—would disrupt continuity and force retraining.

name: Semi-Automated Event Triage Development Pathway and External Collaboration
consequences: Developing the Aim 3 event-triage algorithm in-house (via the computational neuroscience postdoc) preserves IP, ensures methods transparency, and aligns with publication strategy, but requires hiring machine-learning expertise or contracting external consultants, consuming 15–20% of computational budget and deferring results to year 2–3. Alternatively, outsourcing algorithm development to a commercial signal-processing vendor or academic collaborators accelerates delivery but introduces dependency risk, blurs authorship and intellectual property, and may produce a black-box system unsuitable for downstream clinical translation.
options: Fund the in-house postdoctoral researcher to develop the event-triage algorithm using open-source frameworks (e.g., scikit-learn, MNE-Python) with quarterly co-design meetings with clinical staff and published validation against dual-human scoring, accepting 6–9 month delivery lag but retaining full academic ownership.

Establish a formal collaborative agreement with an established sleep signal-processing lab at a partner institution (e.g., Max Planck Institute, Charitée Berlin) to co-develop the algorithm under a joint publication agreement, splitting development costs and accelerating prototyping via their existing ML infrastructure.

Contract a commercial biomedical signal-analysis vendor to build a custom event-classifier module against your labeled dataset, with licensing and non-disclosure restrictions ensuring your team retains training-set ownership and can publish methodological results independently of vendor claims.
review: In-house development preserves scientific autonomy and publication control but delays deployment and risks skill-set gaps; external partnerships accelerate delivery but create IP entanglement and reliance on third-party priorities. The options do not specify how to handle model performance if it underperforms against human adjudication.

name: Participant Selection Stringency and Recruitment Pipeline Efficiency
consequences: Stricter pre-admission criteria (requiring documented prior PSG showing a parasomnia event, collateral bed-partner history, and structured clinical interview) reduce false-positive admissions and raise event-capture yield per participant, but narrow the recruitment pool and slow enrollment velocity, risking the 50–70 target by year 3. Relaxed criteria (accepting self-reported parasomnia history alone, even without prior PSG) accelerate recruitment and meet enrollment targets faster but increase the proportion of participants with sub-threshold or psychogenic events, diluting Aim 2 phenotyping and inflating the 20% unproductive admission ceiling.
options: Enforce a two-stage screening model: all referrals undergo structured telephone clinical interview and collateral contact; only those with high pre-test probability (either prior PSG confirmation or witnessed partner corroboration plus ≥2 episodes per month) are invited for in-person pre-admission assessment, deferring enrollment to participants who pass both gates.

Accept self-reported parasomnia history as the sole entry criterion, enrolling broadly to maximize recruitment velocity, then stratify post-hoc analysis by sub-groups (prior PSG confirmed vs. clinical suspicion only, witnessed vs. unconfirmed) to isolate true parasomnia signal from psychogenic mimics and allow sensitivity analysis.

Implement a dynamic enrollment pipeline where the first 25 participants follow rigorous prior-PSG requirement, and months 6–18 shift to clinical-interview-only admission to stress-test how many captured events come from the less-stringent cohort, using the difference to inform a mid-program protocol amendment.
review: Stringent criteria reduce false admissions but slow enrollment and risk missing the 50–70 target; relaxed criteria accelerate throughput but dilute event yield and complicate phenotyping interpretation. The options do not reconcile how to handle participants who report 2+ events per month historically but produce none during their stay.

name: Sensing Infrastructure Depth and Data Curation Labor
consequences: The tiered sensing model (low-burden nightly monitoring plus escalation PSG) captures continuous contextual data but generates terabytes of video, audio, and sensor streams requiring real-time annotation triage and post-hoc curation—a labor-intensive bottleneck that consumes scorer time and creates privacy-sensitive storage obligations. Reducing to nightly EEG headband and mattress sensor alone (excluding video/audio) cuts annotation burden by ~50% and eliminates bedroom privacy concerns, but loses micromotion and vocalization phenotypes that may discriminate parasomnia subtypes and complicate Aim 3 algorithm benchmarking against multimodal ground truth.
options: Retain full tiered sensing with video and audio escalation deployment, but restrict video/audio storage and annotation strictly to flagged event windows (30 seconds pre/post) rather than entire nights, reducing retention burden to <2% of raw stream and enabling high-resolution event morphology study while minimizing privacy and storage overhead.

Deploy nightly EEG headband and mattress sensors without video or audio except during scheduled enhanced nights (first, mid-stay, final), treating full polysomnography nights as the only multi-modal capture events, accepting reduced event granularity for single-instance admissions but preserving three high-resolution reference points per participant.

Implement a real-time sensor-fusion decision rule where audio-only (no video) is captured every night, analyzed by an automated vocalization detector during escalation, and human review is triggered only if the detector flags night-terror vocalizations or confusional-speech patterns, drastically reducing manual review while preserving voice phenotyping.
review: Full multimodal sensing maximizes phenotypic detail but creates privacy liability and annotation bottleneck; minimal sensing reduces labor but sacrifices phenotypic granularity and complicates algorithm training. The options do not address how to maintain participant anonymity once video and audio exist, even if restricted.

name: Control Group Recruitment and Baseline Data Strategy
consequences: A matched control cohort (healthy adults without parasomnia history) undergoes identical 2–8 week residential monitoring, providing ground-truth baseline for normal arousal patterns, nocturnal movement, and sensor false-positive rates—essential for Aim 3 algorithm specificity benchmarking. However, controls are harder to recruit and retain (no clinical motivation), incur identical per-night compensation and bed-occupancy cost (~€80 per night × 8 weeks × 20 controls = €12.8K), and delay resource availability for the primary parasomnia cohort, compressing the 50–70 patient target unless recruitment timeline is extended.
options: Enroll a full matched control group (20 controls) in parallel with the patient cohort, maintaining 1:2.5 or 1:3 control-to-patient ratio across the 3-year program, and schedule controls for shorter 2–3 week stays to reduce occupancy cost while still capturing sufficient nocturnal cycles for baseline sensor calibration.

Defer control recruitment to year 2 after Aim 2 patient cohort stabilizes, using year-one data to finalize control-matching criteria (age, sex, BMI, sleep duration) and reducing recruitment burden by enrolling a smaller focused control group (8–10 controls) matched to the most prevalent patient phenotypes.

Replace full-length residential control stays with single 1–2 night calibration admissions for 15–20 controls, limiting costs but accepting coarser baseline data and requiring post-hoc statistical adjustment for control representativeness in Aim 3 specificity calculations.
review: Full controls maximize algorithmic specificity benchmarking but strain the 3-year budget and divert bed capacity; deferred or abbreviated controls reduce cost but compromise baseline statistical power and delay publication of Aim 3 sensitivity/specificity. The options do not address recruitment of controls in a way that preserves privacy equivalence (same sensor burden) while reducing motivation to comply.

name: Publication Timing and Preliminary Results Dissemination Strategy
consequences: Releasing methods-validation and preliminary Aim 2 findings in year 2 (via conference abstracts or a pilot-cohort manuscript covering the first 20–25 participants) builds credibility, attracts grant reviewers, and justifies year-three funding, but risks premature interpretation if event-capture numbers remain low or inter-rater agreement on borderline cases is suboptimal, potentially inviting methodological criticism that delays adoption. Withholding all papers until year 3, when the full 50–70 cohort and Aim 3 algorithm are complete, maximizes rigor and impact but leaves a 24-month publication vacuum that may erode funder confidence and expose the program to mid-program termination if preliminary data are not circulated.
options: Publish a methods-focused article in year 18 months (after operational validation of the 8-suite facility and enrollment of the first 15–20 participants) emphasizing setup, safety protocols, and preliminary inter-rater reliability, explicitly framed as a pilot-phase report with limited Aim 2 phenotyping claims, reserving comprehensive Aim 2 and Aim 3 papers for year 3.

Submit a conference abstract per calendar year (year 1: methods/safety, year 2: Aim 2 preliminary, year 3: Aim 3 algorithm) to maintain visible momentum without risking full-journal rejection, while simultaneously composing comprehensive journal manuscripts to appear months after the conference, allowing time for peer review and data completion.

Delay all publications until month 32–36, ensuring data completeness and mature event-triage model, but prepare a detailed written progress report for the external advisory board and DFG program officer every 6 months to maintain funder confidence and create a defensible record of progress should mid-program review occur.
review: Early publication builds funder confidence and institutional visibility but risks undermining credibility if preliminary findings are contradicted by complete data; delayed publication ensures rigor but may trigger skepticism if no peer-reviewed output appears during the 36-month window. The options do not specify how to handle negative findings (e.g., low event-capture rates) that would benefit publication as cautionary methodological evidence.
